content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly 3-12 Writing Rubrics — Introduction and Common Rubric Mis-Steps

Hi, I'm Kristina Smekens. Thanks for joining me for the TEACH writing PD mini-series. In this episode, we're talking about utilizing rubrics with intermediate and secondary writers.

Now I recognize that there is a huge difference between a rubric used with 8-year-olds versus one used with 18-year-olds. However, the purpose and process for building a writing rubric is the SAME. Consequently, this episode IS appropriate for teachers working with writers in grades 3-12. (If you work with Level 1 or 2 English Language learners or special-needs students or those who communicate predominantly in pictures and words — you will likely find the PRIMARY version of this video a more relevant resource.)

Teaching writing isn't just about providing direct instruction; it's also about offering customized feedback. While writer conferences are A HUGE component of growing writers, they can't be the only means of propelling students to improve their writing. With only one teacher and 20 plus students, we need another way for STUDENTS to assess their OWN writing — independent of us.

This is when many attempt to integrate a rubric into their writing classrooms. And although their intentions are good, many make a few key mis-steps in the process.

MIS-STEP #1 — Teachers often turn to the internet for a ready-made rubric. While there ARE some good examples out there, many are not so great. These "bad" rubrics might have too many levels — or too few, have weak or inconsistent criteria, or use too much teacher jargon, making them less than kid friendly. While these may be a source of inspiration, don't plan on "finding" your class writing rubric online.

A second MIS-STEP is when teachers plan to use the state writing rubric as their daily assessment tool. While this might seem like a good idea — since it's what students will be assessed on — by and large, state rubrics are too long, are loaded with teacher jargon, and represent the END-of-year goal. We need a tool that is SHORTER, uses kid-friendly language, and represents current writing goals.

This leads some teachers to make up their own rubric. And that's MIS-STEP #3. Any skill that WE put on the rubric is presumptive. If students didn't notice the skill, name the skill, and describe its application, then it's hardly fair to assess them on it within an instructional rubric.

So, if you aren't to find it, revise it, or make it — How DO you acquire a kid-friendly, instructional writing rubric? YOU build it — WITH your students!

Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly 3-12 Writing Rubrics — Six Characteristics of Strong Rubrics

This is the first of 6 characteristics of strong rubrics:

#1 — You generate instructional rubrics WITH the students. This is perhaps the most important rule. An instructional writing rubric is not made by the teacher, nor is it found online. It's made FOR and WITH your students. This isn't a suggestion; this is best practice.

Research shows that students are more engaged and motivated when they help set their own academic goals and can gauge their progress. When students help create the rubric, they better understand it. This collaborative approach ensures students are active participants in their learning and ultimately more independent in assessing and improving their own writing.

Now, for those who teach multiple SECTIONS of writing, plan to BUILD a rubric with each class period, but then MERGE the criteria into a single document. This fosters student ownership PER class, but also leaves YOU with a single assessment tool.

Follow this same approach EVEN if you teach multiple GRADE levels. YES, the same criteria CAN fit various grade levels — in fact, that's what most state assessment rubrics do. They have a rubric for grades 3-5 and another for 6-12.

#2 — The 2nd characteristic of a strong rubric is that it has multiple levels. To be a rubric, the tool has to have at least 3 levels, although it's MORE common for writing rubrics to have 4, 5, or 6. And of those, there is at least 1 that honors those who are EXCEEDING the goal. The others are MEETING expectations or below.

#3 — THIRD, explicit criteria describes the quality of writing at each level. Let me say that another way — this is not a rubric, it's a Likert scale. While it DOES include more than 3 levels, it only details what the writing skills look like if they are all met. A strong writing rubric addresses the SAME writing skills ACROSS the high, middle, and low levels. This makes the ingredients parallel and establishes a much more objective assessment tool.

#4 — The criteria described within the rubric should mirror the skills outlined within grade-level writing standards. That's characteristic number 4. The criteria on a writing rubric must target persuasive, argumentative, informative, and narrative writing skills, as well as language and convention standards.

#5 — Another key element of effective instructional rubrics is the use of concrete examples. This could be as simple as embedding specific words and phrases within different criteria, or include an evolving piece of writing that depicts what high, middle, and low looks like at the different levels.

#6 — The 6th characteristic of INSTRUCTIONAL rubrics is that they are always GROWING. It's common that the beginning-of-year rubric is relatively sparse. Since you haven't taught or reviewed much, there isn't much to hold students accountable for. However, as you teach more skills, you update the rubric criteria raising the bar of your grading expectations. This demonstrates that our writing instruction is cumulative; students are not learning writing skills in isolation to then forget about them in the next unit. Rather, writing skills are applicable ACROSS genres and are to be applied in ALL future writings. We aren't CHANGING the rubric expectations throughout the year — we are GROWING them.

section_name: Data Collection Rubrics vs. Instructional Rubrics
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly 3-12 Writing Rubrics — Data Collection Rubrics vs. Instructional Rubrics

Now, don't be confused. There ARE rubrics that never change — like the STATE assessment writing rubric. However, this serves a different purpose — it's for DATA COLLECTION.

The expectations or criteria on these rubrics are consistent — THEY never change. Data collection rubrics are used by teachers AFTER students finish writing. They also TYPICALLY provide a HOLISTIC score, meaning the student's writing gets a single score that evaluates the quality of the overall content and ideas. (There is usually a second rubric that scores the language conventions separately.)

These data collection rubrics DO have a place in our curriculum. Beyond our state rubrics, we see them used on EOC assessments and district-wide common assessments. But since they are used by test scorers, administrators, and teachers, they are often complex and wordy, and list ALL the writing skills students should be able to execute by the END of the year. What we need is an ADDITIONAL assessment tool that is student friendly in language, works within the everyday classroom, and is appropriate for the beginning of year.

THIS is the purpose of AN instructional writing rubric.
— It includes only the skills that have been taught.
— And is used by the teacher AND the students.
— The rubric is referenced BEFORE writing, to outline expectations and priorities; DURING writing to intermittently focus and direct revision; and AFTER writing to award a final grade.
— Instructional rubrics typically provide ANALYTIC scores, meaning the piece gets individual scores for EACH component or trait of writing. With individual scores, analytic rubrics indicate WHICH components students are mastering, while identifying those they need further support and instruction.

Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly 3-12 Writing Rubrics — Decisions Before Building a Rubric

Now that we have a common understanding of what an INSTRUCTIONAL rubric is and is NOT, you will want to make some immediate decisions regarding the kid-friendly rubric you will utilize within your classroom.

— Determine the medium and format. Some prefer that the rubric is visible within the physical classroom environment — whether that requires a permanent space on the wall or a portable resource like a trifold poster board. Others are limited on space and prefer that the rubric be an easily-accessible digital resource. Whether you plan to post it or project it, determine the medium you will use for your class instructional rubric.

— Determine the number of levels. Although a rubric must have at LEAST 3 levels, that's usually not enough. Consequently, most teachers are deciding between 4, 5, or 6 levels. Although fewer seems easier to manage, more levels accounts for a wider range of writer abilities.

Here's an option: You could plan to describe 3 levels — the high, middle, low — but then spread them out to have 5 levels. The 2 and 4 would not actually include any detailed criteria. They would simply represent the "in between" score. Like if a student met SOME of the criteria for a Level 5 and some of the criteria for a Level 3, he would earn a Level 4. This provides the efficiency of juggling only 3 sets of criteria but the flexibility of honoring up to 5 different levels.

Regardless if you write out all levels or have some blank "in-betweeners," determine the number of levels YOU want on your class rubric.

— Determine the "TRAITS" to include. If your students are familiar with the 6 Traits of writing, then you can use those as categories on your instructional rubric: ideas, organization, voice, word choice, sentence fluency, and conventions. Or, you can simplify your rubric by combining some into a single category, like "STYLE."

Regardless of your 6 Traits understanding, be sure to separate language conventions FROM message content. THEN, further separate the development of ideas from their organization. Ideas, organization and conventions are the trophy traits on state rubrics. We want to be able to evaluate the content stated, explained, and supported — separately from the overall text structure and organization of information. Again, THIS is one of the greatest advantages of an analytic instructional rubric. We can ANALYZE these ingredients independent of each other.

— THEN determine the small skills that will ULTIMATELY make up the criteria of each trait. Let me clarify — I'm not suggesting you MAKE the rubric yourself before MAKING it with the students. But I do think the process of building a kid-friendly rubric with your classes is made MUCH more efficient if you have SOME idea of the small skills you think should be included.

Identify 1-3 skills per trait. Consider writing skills that you have already TAUGHT or REVIEWED this year. These will be your cheat sheet when guiding students through the actual process of building the rubric.

section_name: Preparing Anchor Papers for Rubric Building
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly 3-12 Writing Rubrics — Preparing Anchor Papers for Rubric Building

And finally, determine the grade-level ANCHOR PAPERS that represent your writers' current abilities. You'll need at least three writing samples that are all on the same topic. Although your tendency might be to grab a high, middle, and low writing from your class, don't use any of your students' actual writing. (Who wants to be the low example!?)

Rather, look for a single example online. Do this by googling for a particular grade level and writing assignment — like "eighth grader essay, fifth grade description, sample 10th grade literary analysis." Find one that represents ANY level of your students. It could be similar to your lowest writers, more like your typical or middle-level writers, or similar to your highest writers.

COPY and paste this sample into AI, prompting it to revise the writing quality to add or remove details, strengthen or weaken word choice, increase or decrease sentence variety. Revise this SAME TOPIC to create representations of each level on your rubric.

Make sure that the HIGHEST anchor paper is SLIGHTLY better than your best writers at this point in the year, and that the lowest anchor paper is no better than your weakest writers are producing at this point. Finally, generate middle-level examples by tweaking the high and low.

And remember if you teach MULTIPLE grade levels, you will likely want to have a set of high, middle, low samples for EACH of your different grade levels.

section_name: Executing the Rubric Lesson with Students
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly 3-12 Writing Rubrics — Executing the Rubric Lesson with Students

Now you are ready to execute the rubric lesson with your students. You might open the mini-lesson like this: "Class, today we are going to BUILD a rubric that you will use to answer the questions you're so often asking me — IS THIS GOOD? AM I DONE? It's normal to question the quality of your own writing, particularly when you're composing it. Therefore, writers need a rubric to determine the CURRENT level of their own writing and how to make it better."

At this point, project or post your rubric template.

— Point out the vertical columns, explaining that rubrics have at least three levels. Identify them by their names listed across the top. I propose using words or descriptive labels rather than numbers. FOR EXAMPLE: just starting, fair, pretty good, good, and great. OR, think about Olympic medals: bronze, silver, gold, platinum, diamond. Even a baseball theme would work: Single, double, triple, home run, grand slam. And if you had six levels, the highest could be labeled as "Grand Slam in the World Series."

(When we identify rubric levels by number, we tend to equate them to points and add up the scores. BUT that is NOT how you calculate grades using a rubric. You don't just add up levels. While the process of calculating grades won't be described until Episode 7, for those wanting that information sooner, check out the hyperlink within the digital handout.)

Point out that the lowest level on the rubric is not a strikeout. It's not bad writing, and it will not be a zero. Remember, you made writing samples to represent all of your writers, including your weakest. Consequently, rubrics will INCLUDE a level that describes weak writing. (Don't get me wrong. A zero is an option for those who don't turn anything in. But the notion of the rubric is that even WEAK writing is still on the board — it's still a base hit. Again, more about scoring and calculating grades will be addressed within Episode 7.)

— If you have chosen a rubric format that includes five levels with 2 that will be blank, then explain why those columns appear skinnier on the template, but still NAME those levels.

After explaining the vertical columns of a rubric, move to the far left and identify the writing traits or categories. Explain that although these are broad, each will eventually include several bulleted criteria that will describe the smaller skills and specific evidence of that trait.

Point out the lines that create separation between the categories. Reveal how this allows for scoring of individual categories.

And finally, reiterate that the rubric you will build today will be used by THEM — even MORE OFTEN than you!

section_name: Four-Step Process for Drafting Rubric Criteria
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly 3-12 Writing Rubrics — Four-Step Process for Drafting Rubric Criteria

Once the format and facets of the rubric are revealed, execute this 4-step process for drafting the criteria.

1. Ask students what writing skills they already know or associate with these different rubric categories. What would fall under the idea development row? What does "organized writing" include? Make a list of the smaller skills your students mention. (This is where YOUR cheat sheet of small skills will be useful.) You can nudge or remind them a little, but remember, if students don't think of the skill to mention it, then they likely don't know it well enough to be assessed on it. Consider including only those writing skills that you have taught or reviewed at this point in the year.

2. Reveal the LOWEST writing sample, the one that you created with your weakest writers in mind. Before reading it, prompt students to listen for how these small skills look and sound within this sample.

3. After reading the low sample, record students' descriptions of each skill using THEIR more-casual language. You can reinforce the ideas with accurate writer vocabulary, but be sure to also include their kid-friendly wording. Remember, this is OUR class rubric — so WE, the students, have to comprehend it, too!

One caution — When students describe a skill as "pathetic" in word choice and "terrible" in organization, educate them on the role of a rubric — It's to honor what was included or attempted. At the very least, rubric criteria is to be neutral over negative. Consequently, guide them to consider synonyms that still imply this is BELOW the goal, but without the negative connotation. For example, the criteria might read "basic" word choice and organization is "hard to follow."

Another tip — When capturing their descriptive criteria, cite particular details, words, lines, or paragraphs from the writing sample that is evidence of that skill. Put these in parentheses at the end of the criteria. This will support a consistent interpretation when using the rubric.

4. After fleshing out the bullets for the LOWEST level, move to the right and reveal the next-highest writing sample. Explain that although this next level will describe the characteristics of slightly-better writing, it will reference the SAME smaller skills per row. Repeat this process until all levels are complete.

section_name: Closing the Rubric Lesson and Key Takeaways
content:
Episode 4 | Kid-Friendly 3-12 Writing Rubrics — Closing the Rubric Lesson and Key Takeaways

Students' participation in creating the rubric criteria is vital! When they rationalize why one sample is better than another, they are signaling that these are skills they KNOW and can be assessed on within their OWN writing.

Once the INITIAL rubric is complete, return to any "blank" levels and clarify how they are earned (by possessing characteristics from two different levels).

End this lesson acknowledging that "This is the INITIAL rubric. It represents the CURRENT writing levels and the next-level goals for students. However, it WILL grow throughout the year. As new skills are taught, they will be added to the class instructional rubric."

This is important for students to know and TEACHERS to RECOGNIZE! Don't fear a skimpy INITIAL rubric. There will be A LOT of additions and UPDATES made all year long. (Again, this process will be explained in Episode 7 of this mini series.)

Additionally, communicate that you are repeating this process with all your classes, and when THESE students come tomorrow, you will reveal the MERGED version of the WRITING RUBRIC.

As the class departs, take a photo or save the digital version as "first period or Section 1" and start your next class revealing the BLANK template only.

As I wrap up this video, let me identify the most important takeaways. Instructional writing rubrics are:
1. TO be generated by the students who will be using it.
2. TO represent ALL of your writers.
3. TO start simple and GROW over time with new instruction.

I encourage you to DETERMINE your rubric format and prepare to BUILD an initial writing rubric for your class. By empowering students with an assessment tool that they helped create, we take the next step toward building better writers.
